title: OpenAI says it has cut attacks that extract its models' hidden reasoning to under 1%
summary: OpenAI cuts attacks extracting model hidden reasoning to under 1 percent
detailed: OpenAI reduced successful attacks extracting hidden model reasoning to under 1% by implementing updated safeguards against adversarial distillation.
Key metrics show attack success dropped from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra for earlier requests, and from 22.9% to 0.9% for current requests.
OpenAI is involved, along with disclosed associations regarding external distillation campaigns linked to DeepSeek and Moonshot AI.
This matters because unauthorized distillation can allow student models to inherit frontier capabilities without safeguards, posing cybersecurity and biological risks.
sentences: 20, that it has sharply cut how often attackers can extract the hidden reasoning of its newest models, publishing its most detailed account yet of how it fights adversarial distillation: the unauthorized use of a frontier model's outputs to train a copy [1].

In an internal adaptive red-teaming test, attacks that tried to recover protected reasoning from an earlier request succeeded 0.2% of the time against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, down from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with its original ones [1].
OpenAI said it is now applying selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra as well [1].

Distillation is a standard machine-learning technique in which a "student" model learns from data produced by a "teacher" model, such as its answers, its reasoning or its judgments about which answers are better [1].

OpenAI argues that, beyond intellectual property, an unauthorized copy can inherit a model's capabilities without its safeguards, so it may help with cyberattacks or biology work the original would refuse [1].
The company puts particular weight on its models' chain-of-thought, the intermediate steps a model generates before answering, which it keeps hidden and shows users only as summaries [1].
In an internal study, OpenAI fine-tuned the same pretrained student on trajectories from Astra-level teachers working on coding and defensive security tasks.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally beat the one trained on summaries; after a round of reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on ExploitBench and SEC-bench Pro, while the summary-trained student did better at lower budgets [1].
OpenAI described defenses at two levels [1].

For individual requests, it trains models to recognize and refuse extraction attempts, runs input classifiers to spot them and output classifiers to catch leaks in both messages and tool-call arguments, and restricts at the API level how encrypted reasoning can be reused [1].

With GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, which launched this week ( our report), protected reasoning is tied to the conversation that produced it: if an earlier message is rewritten, the API drops the reasoning that followed, and older model families cannot read the new models' reasoning [1].
OpenAI said it also closed a pathway that could expose another user's encrypted reasoning [1].

At the campaign level, OpenAI said it has seen multiple unauthorized distillation campaigns on its platform this year, investigates the account networks behind them and shares indicators of compromise with other model providers [1].
The company also announced this week that resellers of access to its models need its approval ( our report); Friday's post cites a consistent-standards policy for providers offering its models [1].

OpenAI said it briefed Congress in February on activity indicating DeepSeek was attempting to distill US frontier models, and in September attributed a core part of a reasoning-extraction campaign to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi [1].
It said it plans to share more about recently disrupted campaigns [1].
